title: OpenPFC Applications
text:
Preface
This report documents the applications shipped with OpenPFC 0.2: what each one solves, how it is discretised, how it is verified, and — where it has been measured — how it scales.
Every chapter follows the same shape. The governing equations come first, in the form a physicist would write them. The discrete formulation follows: for the spectral applications that means the reciprocal-space symbol, and for the finite-difference applications the stencil and update rule. Each chapter then states what is actually verified in the test suite, so a claim in this report can be traced to an assertion in the repository.
The report is written in Quarto. It has no compute engine: the scalability figures are committed SVGs regenerated by figures/make_figures.py from the CSV files under data/, which are themselves transcribed from docs/hpc/lumi_gpu_scaling.md.
quarto render docs/report          # HTML
quarto render docs/report --to pdf # PDF






Status



This is a first draft. The mathematics and verification sections are complete for every shipped application. The scalability chapter covers the three models that have been measured on LUMI-G; the remaining applications are marked as unmeasured rather than estimated.

title: Abstract
text:
OpenPFC is a framework for solving partial differential equations on structured, periodic, MPI-distributed grids, with matching CPU and GPU execution paths. Its original target was the phase-field crystal (PFC) model, but the architecture — a domain decomposition, a distributed field, a pluggable spectral or finite-difference stack, and a session that wires them from JSON — is not specific to PFC.
This report describes the thirteen applications shipped with OpenPFC 0.2. They span fourth- through tenth-order spatial operators, conserved and non-conserved dynamics, dispersive and dissipative behaviour, single-field and coupled multi-field systems, and both spectral and finite-difference discretisations.
Two claims run through the report.
The first is that high differential order is not high implementation complexity in a spectral code. A sixth-order elastohydrodynamic operator and a fourth-order Cahn–Hilliard operator differ, in the source, by the polynomial returned from one function. The equivalent real-space stencils would not be comparable in effort. What high order does cost is stiffness, and the report is explicit about how exponential time differencing absorbs it.
The second is that the same application source runs on a laptop core and on 32 GPUs. Chapter 16  Scalability reports measured strong-scaling curves for three models on LUMI-G, out to 32 GCDs across four nodes, together with the point at which each curve stops being worth extending.
Neither claim is asserted without a number behind it. Where a property has not been measured, the report says so.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.1 What the applications have in common
An OpenPFC application is a small amount of physics on top of a large amount of shared machinery. The machinery is a periodic structured grid decomposed across MPI ranks, a distributed field type that is host- or device-resident, an FFT or finite-difference stack, and a session that assembles them from a JSON input. The physics is typically one header.
For the spectral applications that header supplies three things:
Nothing else. No loops over \(k\), no MPI, no hand-written kernels, and no separate GPU implementation of the physics: the same header is instantiated for the host and device memory spaces.

section: 1.2 Why that shape is the interesting part
text:
1.2 Why that shape is the interesting part
The consequence is that the derivative order of a model is not a measure of how hard it is to implement. Chapter Chapter 7 solves \(\partial_t h = -B\nabla^4 h\) and chapter Chapter 9 solves a sixth-order elastohydrodynamic problem; in the source the difference is that one function returns \(-Bk_{\mathrm{lap}}^2\) and the other returns a cubic in \(k_{\mathrm{lap}}\). Both are pointwise multiplies on a transformed field.
Writing the same two operators as real-space stencils would not be comparable in effort, and the sixth-order stencil would be wide, awkward at the decomposition boundary, and expensive in halo traffic.
What high order does cost is stiffness. The most negative eigenvalue of a \(k^6\) operator on a grid of spacing \(\Delta x\) scales as \(\Delta x^{-6}\), so an explicit integrator’s stable timestep collapses. The applications in this report deal with that by integrating the linear part exactly; chapter Chapter 2 sets out how.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.3 Why not spectral everywhere
Spectral methods buy exactness and simplicity when the problem is periodic and smooth. When it is not, they stop being the right tool. Non-periodic boundaries, sharp interfaces, local transport, and directional-solidification geometry are all better served by high-order finite differences, and OpenPFC supports both under one runtime.
The finite-difference applications in this report exist to make that concrete. heat3d in particular ships both discretisations of the same PDE, which is what makes the comparison in chapter Chapter 16 meaningful: it measures the methods, not two different problems.

title: 2  Numerical methods
text:
2.1 Reciprocal-space convention
Every spectral application is written in terms of the Laplacian symbol
\[
u \;=\; k_{\mathrm{lap}} \;=\; -|\mathbf{k}|^2 ,
\tag{2.1}\]
so that \(\widehat{\nabla^2 \psi} = u\,\hat\psi\) exactly. Using \(u\) rather than \(|\mathbf{k}|\) keeps every operator a polynomial with no square roots: \(\nabla^4 \mapsto u^2\), \(\nabla^6 \mapsto u^3\). It also makes the sign bookkeeping uniform — \(u\) is negative for every mode except \(\mathbf{k}=0\), which is where conservation lives.
A conserved equation is one whose evolution operator carries an explicit factor of \(u\). Because \(u=0\) at \(\mathbf{k}=0\), the mean of the field is then annihilated exactly, not to within a tolerance — a property several application chapters assert bit-exactly rather than numerically.

title: 2  Numerical methods
text:
2.2 Spectral exponential time differencing
The spectral applications share one semi-discrete form. Splitting the right hand side into a part linear in the unknown and a remainder,
\[
\partial_t \hat\psi(\mathbf{k},t)
  = L(k)\,\hat\psi(\mathbf{k},t)
  + M_{\mathrm{nl}}(k)\,\widehat{N[\psi]}(\mathbf{k},t),
\tag{2.2}\]
where \(L\) and \(M_{\mathrm{nl}}\) are pointwise multipliers and \(N\) is evaluated in real space. Integrating the linear part exactly over one step gives the first-order exponential time differencing (ETD1) update
\[
\hat\psi^{\,n+1}
  = e^{L\Delta t}\,\hat\psi^{\,n}
  + \frac{e^{L\Delta t}-1}{L}\,M_{\mathrm{nl}}\,\widehat{N[\psi^{\,n}]},
\tag{2.3}\]
with the coefficient evaluated by its Taylor series where \(|L\Delta t|\) is small enough for the quotient to lose precision.
The point of Equation 2.3 is that all of the stiffness sits inside \(e^{L\Delta t}\), which is a pointwise multiply and is unconditionally stable for \(L<0\) no matter how negative \(L\) becomes. A \(k^{10}\) operator is no less stable than a \(k^2\) one. The timestep is then limited by the nonlinearity and by accuracy, not by the highest derivative in the equation.
The practical size of that effect is worth stating concretely. On a grid with \(\Delta x = 2\pi/8\) the Nyquist wave number is \(k_{\max}=4\), and a sixth-order operator with unit coefficient has \(|L(k_{\max})| \approx 4^6 = 4096\), so forward Euler would need \(\Delta t < 2/|L| \approx 5\times 10^{-4}\). The corresponding tenth-order operator needs \(\Delta t \lesssim 2\times 10^{-6}\). ETD runs both at the timestep the physics wants.
One step therefore costs two transforms — a forward transform of \(N\) and an inverse transform of the updated field — plus \(O(1)\) work per mode.

2.2.1 Dealiasing
Where \(N\) is polynomial, the product raises the highest wave number present: \(\psi^2\) doubles it and \(\psi^3\) triples it. On a finite grid that content folds back onto resolved modes. Applications with a polynomial nonlinearity therefore apply the Orszag 2/3 rule, zeroing the upper third of the spectrum after each nonlinear evaluation. Purely linear applications (Chapter 7) do not need it and switch it off.

title: 2  Numerical methods
text:
2.3 Finite differences
The finite-difference applications discretise derivatives with centred stencils of even order \(2m\), exchanging \(m\) ghost cells per face before each evaluation. OpenPFC provides the halo exchange for host and device fields, including a GPU-aware path that passes device pointers to MPI directly when the installation supports it.
Time stepping is explicit — forward Euler, or a Runge–Kutta scheme where the application needs it — and therefore subject to the usual parabolic condition
\[
\Delta t \;\lesssim\; \frac{\Delta x^2}{2 d\, D}
\tag{2.4}\]
in \(d\) dimensions for a diffusion coefficient \(D\). This is exactly the constraint ETD removes for the spectral applications, and it is why the finite-difference applications in this report are second-order-in-space problems rather than sixth.

title: 2  Numerical methods
text:
2.4 What “verified” means here
Each application chapter ends with a Verification section. The tests behind those sections fall into four kinds, and it is worth distinguishing them:

Analytical — the discrete operator is compared against a closed-form symbol or solution, typically to \(10^{-12}\) or better. This is the strongest kind and most of the spectral applications have one, because a single Fourier mode of a linear operator has an exact answer.
Conservation — a quantity the formulation should preserve is checked, in several cases bit-exactly.
Convergence — the error is measured against a refined or analytic solution across resolutions and the observed order compared to the design order.
Regression — a checksum is pinned so that a change of decomposition, backend, or platform is detected. These catch ports, not physics.

Where an application has only regression coverage for some property, the chapter says so.

title: 3  Tungsten PFC
text:
3.1 Physical setting
Phase-field crystal describes a crystalline solid through a continuous, periodic density field \(\psi(\mathbf{x},t)\) whose minima sit on lattice sites. Because the field is continuous but its ground state is periodic, PFC resolves elasticity, defects, and grain boundaries on diffusive time scales rather than the vibrational scales molecular dynamics is bound to. This application is parameterised for tungsten and is used for solidification and defect studies in three dimensions.

title: 3  Tungsten PFC
text:
3.2 Governing equations
The dynamics are conserved,
\[
\partial_t \psi \;=\; \nabla^2 \frac{\delta F}{\delta \psi},
\tag{3.1}\]
so the spatial mean of \(\psi\) is a constant of the motion. The free energy splits into a quadratic part carrying the two-point correlation and a local remainder,
\[
F[\psi] \;=\; \int \Big[ \tfrac12\,\psi\,\big(C(\nabla^2)\big)\,\psi
                        \;+\; f_{\mathrm{loc}}(\psi,\psi_{\mathrm{MF}}) \Big]\,
          d\mathbf{x}.
\tag{3.2}\]
The local part is a polynomial in \(\psi\) and in a mean-field-filtered density \(\psi_{\mathrm{MF}}\), with coefficients \(p_2,p_3,p_4\) and \(q_{20},\dots,q_{40}\) that encode the solid and vapour branches of the equation of state.

title: 3  Tungsten PFC
text:
3.3 Spectral formulation
Writing \(u = k_{\mathrm{lap}} = -|\mathbf{k}|^2\) as in Section 2.1, the evolution operator is
\[
L(k) \;=\; u\;C(k), \qquad M_{\mathrm{nl}}(k) \;=\; u ,
\tag{3.3}\]
so both the linear and the nonlinear channel carry the conserving factor \(u\).
The correlation symbol \(C(k)\) is built around a peak at \(|\mathbf{k}|=1\), which is what selects the lattice constant. With \(\kappa = |\mathbf{k}|-1\) measuring distance from the peak,
\[
C(k) \;=\; \underbrace{P_{\mathrm{stab}}}_{\text{ETD stabiliser}}
        \;+\; \bar p_2
        \;-\; \underbrace{B_x\,e^{-T/T_0}\,g(\kappa)}_{\text{correlation peak}}
        \;+\; \bar q_2\, f_{\mathrm{MF}}(k),
\tag{3.4}\]
with a deliberately asymmetric peak shape
\[
g(\kappa) \;=\;
\begin{cases}
  \exp\!\big(-\kappa^2/\alpha^2\big), & \kappa < 0 \quad\text{(Gaussian side)},\\[4pt]
  1 - \kappa^2/\alpha^2,              & \kappa \ge 0 \quad\text{(parabolic side)},
\end{cases}
\tag{3.5}\]
and a mean-field filter
\[
f_{\mathrm{MF}}(k) \;=\; e^{\,u/\lambda^2}.
\tag{3.6}\]
Two details in Equation 3.4 matter for the numerics rather than the physics. The \(e^{-T/T_0}\) factor makes the peak depth temperature-dependent, which is how melting enters. The \(P_{\mathrm{stab}}\) term is a constant shift added to \(C\) and subtracted again inside the pointwise nonlinearity; it moves \(L\) away from zero for the modes that would otherwise sit near the stability boundary, which is what lets ETD take a useful timestep. It changes the split, not the solution.
An optional thermal drive \(G_{\mathrm{grid}}\), \(V_{\mathrm{grid}}\) imposes a moving temperature gradient for directional-solidification studies. When omitted the run is isothermal.

title: 3  Tungsten PFC
text:
3.4 Solution strategy
ETD1 as in Equation 2.3, with dealiasing on, one \(\psi\) field and a filtered \(\psi_{\mathrm{MF}}\) derived from it each step. Two transforms per step.
For moving-front studies the application supports a moving boundary condition that tracks the solidification front along \(x\) and shifts the computational window to follow it. The tracked front state — the unwrapped position, the scan index, and a first-detection flag — is part of the checkpoint, so a restarted two-leg run continues the same interface rather than re-detecting it at \(t=0\).

title: 3  Tungsten PFC
text:
3.5 Verification

Split-run equivalence. A checkpoint-and-restart run reproduces an uninterrupted run: local fields agree within \(10^{-12}\) and the saved front state agrees exactly, on one and two MPI ranks (tungsten-moving-restart-2rank).
Golden regression. CPU and 4-rank golden checksums are pinned (tungsten-cpu-golden, tungsten-golden-4rank).
CPU/GPU agreement. SPECTRAL_CHECKSUM from 1 GCD and 16 GCDs agrees to about \(10^{-12}\) relative.
Fail-closed restart. A checkpoint missing front state, or one whose boundary configuration has changed, is a startup error rather than a silent re-detection.

There is no closed-form solution to compare against here — that is the price of a realistic equation of state — so the coverage is regression and self-consistency rather than analytical. The high-order spectral chapters that follow are the ones carrying analytical checks.

title: 4  Aluminium PFC
text:
4.1 Physical setting
The same phase-field crystal picture as Chapter 3: a conserved periodic density whose minima are lattice sites. The differences are the equation of state, an FCC seeding initial condition (seed_grid_fcc), and a moving-frame formulation aimed at directional solidification, where the interesting physics is a front travelling through the domain rather than a bulk relaxation.

title: 4  Aluminium PFC
text:
4.2 Governing equations
Conserved PFC dynamics, as in Equation 3.1:
\[
\partial_t \psi \;=\; \nabla^2 \frac{\delta F}{\delta \psi}.
\]
The free energy has the same structure as Equation 3.2 — a quadratic correlation term plus a local polynomial in \(\psi\) and the mean-field density — with the aluminium coefficients \(\bar p_2,\bar p_3,\bar p_4\) and \(\bar q_{20},\dots,\bar q_{40}\).

title: 4  Aluminium PFC
text:
4.3 Spectral formulation
\[
L(k) \;=\; u\,C(k), \qquad M_{\mathrm{nl}}(k) \;=\; u ,
\qquad u = k_{\mathrm{lap}} = -|\mathbf{k}|^2 .
\tag{4.1}\]
Alongside \(C(k)\) the model carries a separate correlation kernel \(P(k)\) applied to the density each step. The pointwise nonlinearity is therefore a function of four arguments rather than two,
\[
N \;=\; N\big(\psi,\ \psi_{\mathrm{MF}},\ (P*\psi),\ T_{\mathrm{var}}(x,t)\big),
\tag{4.2}\]
where \((P*\psi)\) is the kernel-filtered density — a convolution in real space, hence a multiply in reciprocal space — and \(T_{\mathrm{var}}\) is the imposed temperature field.

title: 4  Aluminium PFC
text:
4.4 Moving frame and thermal drive
The temperature varies in space and time as a travelling profile,
\[
T_{\mathrm{var}}(x,t) \;=\;
  T_0 + G_{\mathrm{grid}}\big(x - x_{\mathrm{initial}} - V_{\mathrm{grid}}\,t\big),
\tag{4.3}\]
clamped between T_min and T_max. A gradient \(G_{\mathrm{grid}}\) pulled through the domain at speed \(V_{\mathrm{grid}}\) is the standard directional-solidification setup: the front settles at the position where the local temperature matches the interface condition, and then travels with the gradient. Setting \(G_{\mathrm{grid}}=0\) recovers an isothermal run at T_const.

title: 4  Aluminium PFC
text:
4.5 Solution strategy
ETD1 as in Equation 2.3, dealiased, with the mean-field filter and the correlation kernel evaluated as reciprocal-space multiplies. Two transforms per step plus the kernel application.

Schema. JSON round-trip and range validation on every parameter.

title: 5  Cahn–Hilliard spinodal decomposition
text:
5.1 Physical setting
An Fe–Cr alloy held at 475 °C inside its chemical spinodal separates spontaneously into Fe-rich and Cr-rich domains. There is no nucleation barrier: every long-wavelength composition fluctuation grows. The technological interest is that this is the mechanism behind “475 °C embrittlement” in ferritic stainless steels, and the length scale of the resulting microstructure sets the mechanical consequence.

title: 5  Cahn–Hilliard spinodal decomposition
text:
5.2 Governing equations
One conserved composition field \(c\) (Cr mole fraction):
\[
\partial_t c \;=\; M\nabla^2\!\left( f'(c) - \kappa\nabla^2 c \right),
\tag{5.1}\]
with the regular-solution bulk free energy in units of \(RT\),
\[
f(c) \;=\; \omega\,c(1-c) \;+\; c\ln c \;+\; (1-c)\ln(1-c),
\qquad \omega = \frac{\Omega}{RT}.
\tag{5.2}\]
The defaults \(T = 748.15\,\mathrm{K}\) and \(\Omega = 20.1\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\) place Fe–32Cr inside the spinodal. This is a documented representative miscibility-gap model, not a CALPHAD assessment, and the report does not claim quantitative agreement with a thermodynamic database.

title: 5  Cahn–Hilliard spinodal decomposition
text:
5.3 Spectral formulation
Linearising the bulk term about the alloy composition \(c_0\) puts \(f''(c_0)\) into the linear symbol and leaves the remainder to the nonlinearity. With \(u = k_{\mathrm{lap}}\),
\[
L(k) \;=\; M\big( f''(c_0)\,u \;-\; \kappa\,u^2 \big),
\qquad
M_{\mathrm{nl}}(k) \;=\; M\,u ,
\tag{5.3}\]
\[
N(c) \;=\; f'(c) - f'(c_0) - f''(c_0)\,(c-c_0).
\tag{5.4}\]
Both channels carry the factor \(u\), so the mean composition is conserved exactly.
The growth rate follows directly from Equation 5.3. Writing \(|\mathbf{k}| = k\),
\[
\lambda(k) \;=\; -M k^2\big( f''(c_0) + \kappa k^2 \big),
\tag{5.5}\]
which is positive — unstable — precisely when \(f''(c_0) < 0\), the spinodal condition. The fastest-growing mode is at \(k_{\max}^2 = -f''(c_0)/(2\kappa)\), and this wavelength is what sets the initial domain spacing.
The nonlinearity Equation 5.4 is not a low-order polynomial — it contains \(\ln\!\big(c/(1-c)\big)\) — so dealiasing is on.

title: 5  Cahn–Hilliard spinodal decomposition
text:
5.4 Solution strategy
ETD1 as in Equation 2.3. Composition is clamped away from \(\{0,1\}\) so the logarithms stay finite; a sampled composition outside the physical range stops the run rather than producing quiet nonsense.
Optional collective CSV diagnostics record mass, composition bounds, and the current-state total energy including the spectral gradient contribution.

title: 5  Cahn–Hilliard spinodal decomposition
text:
5.5 Verification

Analytical growth rate. A single seeded mode grows as \(e^{\lambda(k)t}\) with \(\lambda\) from Equation 5.5, matched within 5%.
Mass conservation. The mean composition is held to \(10^{-12}\) across a run.
Free energy decreases. The total free energy falls monotonically while a spinodal mode grows.
Gradient energy. The diagnostic gradient energy matches the analytical value on distributed grids.
Decomposition independence. Seeded noise produces the same field and the same mean on any number of ranks.

title: 6  Thin-film dewetting and coating
text:
6.1 Physical setting
A thin liquid film on a solid substrate. Two effects compete: surface tension flattens the free surface, and van der Waals interaction with the substrate either thins or thickens the film depending on its local height. Whether a coating levels into a uniform layer or breaks up into droplets is decided by which one wins at which wavelength — a question with obvious relevance to coating processes and to the stability of deposited layers.

title: 6  Thin-film dewetting and coating
text:
6.2 Governing equations
One conserved thickness field \(h\) with constant mobility \(M_0\):
\[
\partial_t h \;=\; \nabla\cdot\big[M_0\nabla p\big],
\qquad
p \;=\; -\gamma\nabla^2 h \;-\; \Pi(h),
\tag{6.1}\]
with the disjoining pressure
\[
\Pi(h) \;=\; A\left[\left(\frac{h_0}{h}\right)^{3}
                   -\left(\frac{h_0}{h}\right)^{9}\right].
\tag{6.2}\]






Sign convention



Some textbook flux forms carry a leading minus that would make the capillary \(k^4\) term destabilising. Equation 6.1 is the standard lubrication balance — flow down the pressure gradient — so short wavelengths damp, which is the physically correct behaviour.


Cubic mobility \(M \propto h^3\) is a local-flux nonlinearity and is deliberately left out of this slice; \(M_0 = M(h_0)\) is exact for the linear band, which is what the verification targets.

title: 6  Thin-film dewetting and coating
text:
6.3 Spectral formulation
With \(u = k_{\mathrm{lap}}\),
\[
L(k) \;=\; -M_0\gamma\,u^2 \;-\; M_0\,\Pi'(h_0)\,u ,
\qquad
M_{\mathrm{nl}}(k) \;=\; -M_0\,u .
\tag{6.3}\]
In terms of \(|\mathbf{k}| = k\) the linear growth rate is
\[
\lambda(k) \;=\; M_0 k^2\big(\Pi'(h_0) - \gamma k^2\big),
\tag{6.4}\]
which is the whole story of the model in one line. The \(-\gamma k^4\) term is capillary damping and always stabilises. The \(+\Pi'(h_0)k^2\) term destabilises when \(\Pi'(h_0) > 0\). Their balance selects a fastest-growing wavelength \(k_{\max}^2 = \Pi'(h_0)/(2\gamma)\), which is the observed droplet spacing in dewetting.
Setting \(A = 0\) removes the disjoining pressure entirely and leaves \(\lambda(k) = -M_0\gamma k^4\): every mode decays, and the film levels. That is the coating limit, and it is a clean analytical target because the decay is exact.

title: 6  Thin-film dewetting and coating
text:
6.4 Solution strategy
ETD1 as in Equation 2.3, dealiased.

title: 6  Thin-film dewetting and coating
text:

Exact \(k^4\) levelling. With \(A=0\), a single mode decays as \(e^{-M_0\gamma k^4 t}\).

Dewetting band. With \(A>0\), modes inside the unstable band grow and those outside decay, with the crossover at the predicted wave number.

title: 7  Surface diffusion
text:
7.1 Physical setting
A rough solid surface held at temperature smooths itself: curvature raises the local chemical potential, adatoms diffuse along the surface from peaks to valleys, and the profile flattens. Mullins derived the small-slope limit in 1957. Industrially this is thermal annealing of nanoscale roughness, and the practical question is how long a given feature size takes to disappear.

title: 7  Surface diffusion
text:
7.2 Governing equations
For a small-slope height profile \(h\),
\[
\partial_t h \;=\; -B\,\nabla^4 h .
\tag{7.1}\]
The chain behind it is: curvature \(\to\) chemical potential \(\mu \propto -\nabla^2 h\), surface flux \(\propto -\nabla\mu\), mass conservation \(\partial_t h = -\nabla\cdot\mathbf{j}\). Two Laplacians from the potential and the divergence give \(\nabla^4\).

title: 7  Surface diffusion
text:
7.3 Spectral formulation
The equation is linear, so the transform diagonalises it completely. With \(u = k_{\mathrm{lap}}\),
\[
L(k) \;=\; -B\,u^2 \;=\; -B|\mathbf{k}|^4 ,
\qquad N \equiv 0 .
\tag{7.2}\]
Every Fourier mode is therefore independent and decays exactly:
\[
h_{\mathbf{k}}(t) \;=\; h_{\mathbf{k}}(0)\,e^{-B|\mathbf{k}|^4 t}.
\tag{7.3}\]
The \(|\mathbf{k}|^4\) in the exponent is the physical content. Halving a feature’s wavelength makes it decay sixteen times faster, so an annealing surface loses its fine structure long before its long-wavelength shape changes. A two-wavelength initial condition separates visibly within a fraction of the long mode’s lifetime.

title: 7  Surface diffusion
text:
7.4 Solution strategy
ETD1 as in Equation 2.3 with \(N \equiv 0\), which reduces Equation 2.3 to \(\hat h^{\,n+1} = e^{L\Delta t}\hat h^{\,n}\) — exact for any \(\Delta t\), to round-off. Dealiasing is off: there is no nonlinearity to alias.
This makes the application a useful correctness probe for the spectral stack itself. Any deviation from Equation 7.3 is a defect in the transform, the decomposition, or the symbol — not discretisation error.

title: 7  Surface diffusion
text:
7.5 Verification

Exact single-mode decay. \(h_k(t) = h_k(0)e^{-Bk^4t}\) to round-off.
Multi-wavelength separation. Two modes decay with the ratio predicted by \(k^4\).
Mean preservation. \(\mathbf{k}=0\) is untouched, so the mean height is exactly constant.

title: 8  Kawahara capillary–gravity waves
text:
8.1 Physical setting
Long weakly nonlinear waves on a shallow fluid layer where surface tension and gravity both matter. Where the Korteweg–de Vries equation keeps only third-order dispersion, Kawahara (1972) retains the fifth-order term as well. When the two have opposite signs they compete, and the resulting dispersion relation is non-monotonic — waves of different length can travel in opposite directions.

title: 8  Kawahara capillary–gravity waves
text:
8.2 Governing equations
\[
\partial_t u \;+\; \alpha\,u\,\partial_x u
  \;-\; \beta\,\partial_x^3 u
  \;+\; \gamma\,\partial_x^5 u \;=\; 0 .
\tag{8.1}\]






Sign convention



This application defines \(\beta\) with a minus sign in Equation 8.1. To use a coefficient \(b\) multiplying \(+u_{xxx}\), set \(\beta = -b\).

title: 8  Kawahara capillary–gravity waves
text:
8.3 Spectral formulation
Odd derivatives transform to odd powers of \(ik\), so the symbol is purely imaginary:
\[
L(k) \;=\; -i\,\omega(k), \qquad \omega(k) \;=\; \beta k^3 + \gamma k^5 .
\tag{8.2}\]
The quadratic flux \(\alpha u\,\partial_x u = \tfrac{\alpha}{2}\partial_x(u^2)\) is evaluated as \(N = u^2\) with
\[
M_{\mathrm{nl}}(k) \;=\; -i\,\frac{\alpha}{2}\,k_x .
\tag{8.3}\]
This is the qualitative difference from every other spectral chapter here. An even-order dissipative operator has \(L\) real and negative: \(|e^{L\Delta t}|<1\) and modes decay. Here \(L\) is imaginary, so \(|e^{L\Delta t}| = 1\) exactly and modes rotate — the amplitude of each Fourier component is preserved and only its phase advances. ETD is not damping anything; it is applying an exact phase rotation.
The phase velocity follows from Equation 8.2:
\[
c_p(k) \;=\; \frac{\omega(k)}{k} \;=\; \beta k^2 + \gamma k^4 ,
\tag{8.4}\]
which changes sign at \(k^2 = -\beta/\gamma\) when \(\beta\gamma < 0\). Below that wave number waves travel one way, above it the other. The defaults \(\alpha = 1\), \(\beta = 1\), \(\gamma = -1\) put the model in this competing regime.

title: 8  Kawahara capillary–gravity waves
text:
8.4 Solution strategy
ETD1 as in Equation 2.3, dealiased — the quadratic nonlinearity doubles the highest wave number present, so the 2/3 rule is required.

Manufactured solutions. Independent manufactured-solution tests for third- and fifth-order dispersion.

title: 9  Elastohydrodynamic film
text:
9.1 Physical setting
A viscous liquid film confined beneath a thin elastic plate. The plate resists bending, that bending sets the pressure in the gap, the pressure gradient drives lubrication flow, and the flow changes the gap. This is the elastohydrodynamic problem behind compliant bearings, soft contacts, and adhesive films — anywhere a thin fluid layer is bounded by something that deforms.

title: 9  Elastohydrodynamic film
text:
9.2 Governing equations
\[
p \;=\; B\nabla^4 h \;-\; \gamma\nabla^2 h \;-\; \Pi(h),
\qquad
\partial_t h \;=\; \nabla\cdot\big[M_0\nabla p\big].
\tag{9.1}\]
The chain is worth reading in order: plate curvature \(\to\) bending pressure (\(B\nabla^4h\)) \(\to\) pressure gradient \(\to\) viscous flux \(\to\) \(\partial_t h\). The bending term is already fourth order, and the divergence of the flux adds two more, so the evolution operator is \(\nabla^6\).

title: 9  Elastohydrodynamic film
text:
9.3 Spectral formulation
With \(u = k_{\mathrm{lap}}\),
\[
L(k) \;=\; M_0 B\,u^3 \;-\; M_0\gamma\,u^2 \;-\; M_0\Pi'(h_0)\,u ,
\qquad
M_{\mathrm{nl}}(k) \;=\; -M_0\,u .
\tag{9.2}\]
In terms of \(|\mathbf{k}| = k\),
\[
\lambda(k) \;=\; -M_0 B k^6 \;-\; M_0\gamma k^4 \;+\; M_0\Pi'(h_0)k^2 .
\tag{9.3}\]
The defaults \(A = \gamma = 0\) leave pure bending relaxation, \(\lambda = -M_0Bk^6\), which is an exact analytical target.

title: 9  Elastohydrodynamic film
section: 9.4 Why this chapter is the stiffness argument
text:
9.4 Why this chapter is the stiffness argument
Equation 9.3 is where the case for ETD is easiest to see. An explicit step on a grid of spacing \(\Delta x\) would require
\[
\Delta t \;\lesssim\; \frac{\Delta x^6}{M_0 B\,\pi^6},
\tag{9.4}\]
a sixth power of the mesh size. Halving \(\Delta x\) costs a factor of 64 in timestep on top of the factor of \(2^d\) in cells per step. ETD treats the \(k^6\) operator as a pointwise multiply by \(e^{L\Delta t}\), which is unconditionally stable, and the timestep is then set by accuracy and by the nonlinearity instead.
The implementation difference between this sixth-order model and the fourth-order Chapter 6 is one extra term in Equation 9.2.

text:
9.5 Solution strategy
ETD1 as in Equation 2.3, dealiased.

Two-mode ratio of 64. Doubling the wave number multiplies the decay rate by \(2^6 = 64\); the measured ratio matches.

title: 10  Higher-order PFC correlation kernel
text:
10.1 Physical setting
The correlation peak of Chapter 3 sits at a single wave number, and that is what fixes the lattice constant. A real liquid-state direct correlation function has more structure than one peak, and capturing a second peak gives control over which crystal symmetry is selected — square rather than triangular in two dimensions, FCC rather than BCC in three.
This application implements a two-mode kernel to make that control explicit, and to serve as the report’s limiting case for derivative order.

title: 10  Higher-order PFC correlation kernel
text:
10.2 Governing equations
Conserved dynamics as in Equation 3.1, with
\[
F[\psi] = \int\Big[\tfrac12\,\psi\,\Lambda(\nabla^2)\,\psi
                   - \tfrac{g}{3}\psi^3 + \tfrac14\psi^4\Big]\,d\mathbf{x},
\qquad
\partial_t\psi = M\nabla^2\frac{\delta F}{\delta\psi}.
\tag{10.1}\]
The two-mode kernel is a product of two Swift–Hohenberg factors,
\[
\Lambda(\nabla^2) \;=\; -\varepsilon
  \;+\; (1+\nabla^2)^2\Big[\,r_1 + (q_1^2+\nabla^2)^2\Big].
\tag{10.2}\]
Each factor contributes \(\nabla^4\), so Equation 10.2 contains \((\nabla^2)^4\) — eighth order in space. Conserved dynamics applies one more Laplacian, so the evolution operator runs through \((\nabla^2)^5\): tenth order.

title: 10  Higher-order PFC correlation kernel
text:
10.3 Spectral formulation
With \(u = k_{\mathrm{lap}} = -|\mathbf{k}|^2\), writing \(a = q_1^2\), \(A = r_1 + a^2\), \(B = 2a\), \(C = 1\), the kernel expands to a quartic in \(u\):
\[
\Lambda(u) = (A-\varepsilon) + (B+2A)\,u + (C+2B+A)\,u^2
             + (2C+B)\,u^3 + C\,u^4 ,
\tag{10.3}\]
and the conserved evolution symbol is one power higher:
\[
L(u) \;=\; M\,u\,\Lambda(u),
\qquad
M_{\mathrm{nl}}(u) \;=\; M\,u,
\qquad
N(\psi) \;=\; \psi^3 - g\psi^2 .
\tag{10.4}\]
Both are evaluated by Horner’s rule on a coefficient array. The implementation carries no special case for \(k^8\) or \(k^{10}\): a single PolynomialInKLap<N> helper serves both, and the entire tenth-order operator is a five-term loop. This is the report’s central architectural claim (Chapter 2) at its limit.
Multiplying by \(u\) shifts every coefficient up one power, which leaves the constant term of \(L\) a literal zero. Mass conservation is therefore exact in the strict sense — \(L(k{=}0)\) is bit-exactly \(0\), and the test asserts == 0.0 rather than a tolerance.

title: 10  Higher-order PFC correlation kernel
text:
10.4 Band structure
\(\Lambda\) has a minimum wherever a factor of Equation 10.2 vanishes: at \(|\mathbf{k}| = 1\) with depth \(-\varepsilon\), and at \(|\mathbf{k}| = q_1\) with depth \(-\varepsilon + (1-q_1^2)^2 r_1\). Setting n_modes = 1 selects the classical fourth-order kernel \(-\varepsilon + (1+\nabla^2)^2\), which has one minimum only.
Growth requires \(\Lambda < 0\), so \(r_1\) controls how much of the second band survives. For two-dimensional square ordering \(q_1 = \sqrt2\) — the \((10)\) and \((11)\) families; for three-dimensional FCC, \(q_1 = 2/\sqrt3\).

The fourth-order kernel cannot place power at \(|\mathbf{k}| = \sqrt2\): it has no minimum there. The eighth-order kernel opens that band, and \(r_1\) tunes the balance continuously, converging back onto the single-mode result as it grows. The \(|\mathbf{k}| = \sqrt3\) band stays empty throughout, so the ordering is the square \((10)+(11)\) family rather than triangular.
Two results here are worth stating plainly because they are easy to assume wrongly. At \(r_1 = 0\) the two minima are exactly degenerate, and the \(\sqrt2\) family then wins outright — its ring carries more modes in two dimensions. That is mathematically tidy but is not a square lattice; \(r_1 = 0.02\) is the value that populates both families. And from random noise on a periodic box the outcome is polycrystalline — several square-ordered grains at different orientations — not a single crystal.

title: 10  Higher-order PFC correlation kernel
text:
10.6 Solution strategy
ETD1 as in Equation 2.3, dealiased because the local term is cubic.
This model is where the stiffness argument of Chapter 2 is sharpest. On the shipped grid \(|L(k_{\max})| \approx 7\times10^{5}\), so forward Euler would require \(\Delta t \approx 3\times10^{-6}\). The application runs at \(\Delta t = 0.05\) — four orders of magnitude larger — because ETD integrates the linear operator exactly.
The mean density is a control parameter rather than a detail. About a nonzero \(\bar\psi\) the effective rate is \(\sigma(k) = Mu\,[\Lambda(u) + n'(\bar\psi)]\) with \(n'(\psi) = 3\psi^2 - 2g\psi\). At \(\bar\psi = -0.05\), \(g = 0.5\) that leaves \(\sigma(|k|{=}1) = 0.19\); at \(\bar\psi = -0.15\) only \(0.033\), and ordering takes roughly six times longer.

title: 10  Higher-order PFC correlation kernel
text:
10.7 Verification

Analytical kernel. \(\Lambda(u)\) matches the factored form to \(10^{-12}\) over \(0 \le |\mathbf{k}| \le 4\), and its five coefficients equal the expansion Equation 10.3.
Tenth order. \(L\) is quintic in \(u\) with a nonzero leading coefficient and equals \(Mu\Lambda(u)\) pointwise.
Exact conservation. \(L\)’s constant term is bit-exactly zero.
Band structure. Degenerate minima at \(r_1 = 0\); the offset is exactly \((1-q_1^2)^2 r_1\) otherwise; the unstable band is exactly where \(\Lambda < 0\).
Order comparison. The \(k^8\) kernel destabilises \(|\mathbf{k}| = \sqrt2\); the \(k^4\) kernel does not.
Growth and stability. An ETD run reproduces \(e^{L(k)t}\) at \(|\mathbf{k}| = 1\) to \(10^{-6}\), holds the mean to \(10^{-13}\), and stays bounded at \(\Delta t\) more than 1000× the explicit limit.

title: 11  Strain-gradient elasticity
text:
11.1 Physical setting
Classical linear elasticity has no intrinsic length scale, so it predicts singular strain fields at idealised defects — a dislocation core, a sharp crack tip — where the real material has a finite structure. Aifantis-type gradient elasticity introduces an internal length \(\ell\) that regularises exactly those features while leaving the far field classical. It is the continuum answer to “what happens below the scale where continuum elasticity stops making sense”.

title: 11  Strain-gradient elasticity
text:
11.2 Governing equations
A Helmholtz operator applied to the Navier operator:
\[
\big(1 - \ell^2\nabla^2\big)\,L_{\mathrm{Navier}}\,\mathbf{u} \;=\; \mathbf{f},
\tag{11.1}\]
which is fourth order in the displacement \(\mathbf{u}\). Features much smaller than \(\ell\) are smoothed; features much larger than \(\ell\) are unaffected, and the \(\ell \to 0\) limit recovers classical elasticity.

title: 11  Strain-gradient elasticity
text:
11.3 Spectral formulation
For constant isotropic moduli on a periodic grid, Equation 11.1 becomes an independent \(2\times2\) linear system at each \(\mathbf{k}\) — no iteration and no time stepping. Splitting the transformed body force into components parallel and perpendicular to \(\mathbf{k}\),
\[
\hat{\mathbf{u}}_L \;=\; \frac{\hat{\mathbf{f}}_L}{-\alpha(\lambda+2\mu)k^2},
\qquad
\hat{\mathbf{u}}_T \;=\; \frac{\hat{\mathbf{f}}_T}{-\alpha\mu k^2},
\tag{11.2}\]
with the gradient factor
\[
\alpha \;=\; 1 + \ell^2 k^2 \quad\text{(fourth order)},
\tag{11.3}\]
and optional sixth-order stretches \(\alpha = (1+\ell^2k^2)^2\) or \(\alpha = 1 + \ell^2k^2 + \ell_4^4k^4\). The \(\mathbf{k}=0\) mode is projected to \(\hat{\mathbf{u}} = 0\), which fixes the rigid-body translation the periodic problem leaves undetermined.
Separating longitudinal from transverse components is what makes the system diagonal: the two polarisations decouple, and each is a scalar divide.

title: 11  Strain-gradient elasticity
text:
11.4 Eigenstrain loading
A two-dimensional dilatational eigenstrain \(\varepsilon^* = \varepsilon_0\,g\,I\) is equivalent to the body force
\[
\mathbf{f} \;=\; \nabla\cdot\big(C:\varepsilon^*\big)
            \;=\; 2(\lambda+\mu)\,\varepsilon_0\,\nabla g .
\tag{11.4}\]
For a cosine inclusion \(g = A\cos(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{x})\) the displacement is the sine field \(\mathbf{u} = B\,\mathbf{k}\sin(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{x})\) with \(B\) known in closed form — which is the analytical target the tests use.

title: 11  Strain-gradient elasticity
text:
11.5 Solution strategy
One shot, not ETD. Forward transform the body force, solve Equation 11.2 at each mode, inverse transform. Two transforms per component, no time loop, no stability condition.
This is worth stating plainly because it shows the spectral stack is not tied to time stepping: the same domain, field, and FFT machinery serves an elliptic solve.

title: 11  Strain-gradient elasticity
text:
11.6 Verification

Analytical displacement. The computed \(\mathbf{u}\) matches the closed-form Fourier solution for a cosine eigenstrain.
Classical limit. \(\ell \to 0\) recovers the classical Navier result.
High-\(k\) reduction. Short-wavelength response is suppressed by the \(\alpha\) factor as designed.
Zero mean. \(\langle\mathbf{u}\rangle = 0\) exactly, from the \(\mathbf{k}=0\) projection.

text:
12.1 Physical setting
Linear diffusion. The physics is not the point: this application exists so that finite-difference order, spectral treatment, timing, and scaling can be compared without the comparison being confounded by a difference in the problem.

title: 12  Heat equation in three dimensions
text:
12.2 Governing equations
\[
\partial_t u \;=\; D\,\nabla^2 u
\tag{12.1}\]
on a periodic box, with a single fixed \(D\) shared by every binary so their errors against the analytic solution are directly comparable.
For a single Fourier mode the exact solution is
\[
u_{\mathbf{k}}(t) \;=\; u_{\mathbf{k}}(0)\,e^{-D|\mathbf{k}|^2 t},
\tag{12.2}\]
which every driver is measured against.
crumbs: 12  Heat equation in three dimensions

title: 12  Heat equation in three dimensions
text:
12.3 Finite-difference formulation
Centred stencils of even order \(2m\) approximate the Laplacian,
\[
\partial_{xx}u\big|_i \;\approx\; \frac{1}{\Delta x^2}\sum_{j=-m}^{m} a_j\,u_{i+j},
\tag{12.3}\]
with \(m\) ghost cells exchanged per face before each evaluation. Orders 2 through 20 are available. Time stepping is explicit, subject to Equation 2.4.
crumbs: 12  Heat equation in three dimensions

title: 12  Heat equation in three dimensions
text:
12.4 Spectral formulation
The spectral drivers use the same reciprocal-space convention as the rest of the report. With \(u = k_{\mathrm{lap}}\) the operator is simply \(L(k) = D\,u\), and the implicit Euler driver applies
\[
\hat u^{\,n+1} \;=\; \frac{\hat u^{\,n}}{1 - \Delta t\,D\,u},
\tag{12.4}\]
which is two transforms per step and unconditionally stable.

12.6 Solution strategy
Explicit stepping for the FD drivers under Equation 2.4; implicit Euler in Fourier space for the spectral drivers, at two transforms per step.
The trade is the usual one. The FD step is cheap and local — a stencil plus a halo exchange with nearest neighbours — but the stable timestep shrinks as \(\Delta x^2\). The spectral step is unconditionally stable but costs two all-to-all transforms, which is global communication. Which wins depends on the accuracy required and on how well the machine’s network carries an FFT transpose; Chapter 16 measures exactly that.

title: 13  Two-dimensional wave equation
text:
13.1 Physical setting
Acoustic propagation on a two-dimensional slab. The application is the smallest shipped example of two prognostic fields advanced together, and of a domain that is periodic in one direction and physically bounded in the other.

title: 13  Two-dimensional wave equation
text:
13.2 Governing equations
The second-order wave equation \(u_{tt} = c^2\nabla^2 u\) is written as a coupled first-order system in displacement and velocity:
\[
\partial_t u \;=\; v,
\qquad
\partial_t v \;=\; c^2\,\nabla^2 u ,
\tag{13.1}\]
with \(\nabla^2 = \partial_{xx} + \partial_{yy}\) on an \(n_z = 1\) slab.
Writing it this way is what lets a single stepper advance a tuple of increments \((\mathrm{d}u, \mathrm{d}v)\), which is the pattern any multi-field application reuses.

title: 13  Two-dimensional wave equation
text:
13.3 Boundary conditions
Periodic in \(x\), handled by MPI halo exchange. In \(y\) the slab is physically bounded, with homogeneous Dirichlet (\(u = 0\)) or Neumann (\(\partial_y u = 0\)) conditions applied as a ghost-cell correction after the periodic exchange.
The ordering matters: the exchange is unconditional and the physical correction overwrites the ghost values it produced on the boundary faces. This keeps the mixed case from needing a separate communication pattern.

title: 13  Two-dimensional wave equation
text:
13.4 Finite-difference formulation
Centred stencils, either a fixed second-order Laplacian (wave2d_fd_manual) or even orders 2–20 (wave2d_fd). The Laplacian components are accumulated as unscaled stencil sums and multiplied by \(1/\Delta x^2\), \(1/\Delta y^2\) in the model’s right-hand side, which keeps the stencil evaluator independent of the grid metric.
Time stepping is explicit, with the hyperbolic CFL condition
\[
\Delta t \;\lesssim\; \frac{1}{c}\left(\frac{1}{\Delta x^2}
                                     + \frac{1}{\Delta y^2}\right)^{-1/2}.
\tag{13.2}\]
Note this is \(\Delta t \sim \Delta x\), not the \(\Delta x^2\) of a parabolic problem: a wave equation is far less stiff than a diffusion equation at the same resolution, and much less stiff than the high-order operators in the spectral chapters.

title: 14  Allen–Cahn
text:
14.1 Physical setting
A two-phase system relaxing toward equilibrium by moving its interfaces. Unlike the Cahn–Hilliard model of Chapter 5, the order parameter here is not conserved: a grain can shrink and vanish. This is the standard model for curvature-driven grain growth.

title: 14  Allen–Cahn
text:
14.2 Governing equations
\[
\partial_t \phi \;=\; M\nabla^2\phi
                 \;-\; \frac{1}{\varepsilon^2}\big(\phi^3 - \phi\big)
                 \;+\; F ,
\tag{14.1}\]
where \(\varepsilon\) sets the interface width, the double-well term \(\phi^3-\phi\) drives \(\phi\) toward \(\pm1\), and \(F\) is an optional constant driving force.

title: 14  Allen–Cahn
text:
14.3 Conserved versus non-conserved
The contrast with Equation 5.1 is the clearest illustration in this report of what the outer \(\nabla^2\) does. Cahn–Hilliard reads \(\partial_t c = M\nabla^2(\dots)\) and is conserved: in reciprocal space every term carries the factor \(u\), so the \(\mathbf{k}=0\) mode is annihilated and the mean cannot move.
Equation 14.1 has no outer Laplacian on the reaction term. Its \(\mathbf{k}=0\) component is \(-\varepsilon^{-2}(\phi^3-\phi) + F\), which is generally nonzero, so \(\langle\phi\rangle\) evolves freely. Physically: Cahn–Hilliard redistributes a fixed amount of solute, Allen–Cahn converts one phase into another.
The consequence for verification is that the natural check is not conservation but the growth of a favoured phase — which is what the test asserts.

title: 14  Allen–Cahn
text:
14.4 Finite-difference formulation
A second-order five-point Laplacian in \(x\) and \(y\) on a periodic slab, with separated halo exchange, and explicit forward Euler:
\[
\phi^{\,n+1}_i \;=\; \phi^{\,n}_i \;+\; \Delta t\left[
   M\,(\nabla^2_h\phi^{\,n})_i
- \frac{1}{\varepsilon^2}\big((\phi^{\,n}_i)^3 - \phi^{\,n}_i\big)
+ F \right].
\tag{14.2}\]
Two stability limits apply: the diffusive condition Equation 2.4, and a reaction condition \(\Delta t \lesssim \varepsilon^2\) from the stiff double well. A sharp interface is therefore expensive, which is the usual phase-field trade-off and the reason \(\varepsilon\) is a numerical as well as a physical parameter.

title: 14  Allen–Cahn
text:
14.5 Solution strategy
Explicit Euler with separated halos, so the stencil evaluation and the halo exchange are distinct phases. Optional PNG snapshots of \(\phi\).

title: 14  Allen–Cahn
text:
14.6 Verification

Superlevel-set growth. The area with \(\phi\) above a threshold grows by at least a prescribed factor between \(t=0\) and the end of the run — the non-conserved counterpart to a conservation check.
CPU–GPU parity. Where CUDA/HIP twins are built.

title: 15  Kobayashi dendritic solidification
text:
15.1 Physical setting
A crystal growing into an undercooled melt. Latent heat released at the moving interface warms the surrounding liquid and suppresses further growth there, while protrusions reach into colder melt and grow faster. That feedback is the origin of dendrites, and the direction they select comes from the anisotropy of the interfacial energy.
Two-way coupling is essential: the phase field moves the temperature through latent heat, and the temperature moves the phase field through the driving force.

title: 15  Kobayashi dendritic solidification
text:
15.2 Governing equations
\[
\tau\,\partial_t\phi \;=\;
    \partial_y\big(\epsilon\,\epsilon'\,\partial_x\phi\big)
  - \partial_x\big(\epsilon\,\epsilon'\,\partial_y\phi\big)
  + \epsilon^2\nabla^2\phi
  + \phi(1-\phi)\!\left(\phi - \tfrac12 + M(T)\right),
\tag{15.1}\]
\[
\partial_t T \;=\; \nabla^2 T \;+\; \kappa\,\partial_t\phi .
\tag{15.2}\]
The interfacial energy \(\epsilon\) depends on the orientation of the interface normal, and \(\epsilon'\) is its derivative with respect to that angle. The first two terms of Equation 15.1 are the anisotropy: they vanish for isotropic \(\epsilon\) and are what makes dendrite arms select particular directions rather than growing as a disc.
\(M(T)\) is the temperature-dependent driving force, and \(\kappa\) is the latent heat coefficient coupling Equation 15.1 back into Equation 15.2.

title: 15  Kobayashi dendritic solidification
text:
15.3 Finite-difference formulation
Second-order centred stencils on a periodic torus in \(x\) and \(y\). The anisotropy terms need the interface normal, so gradients of \(\phi\) are evaluated before the divergence-like terms are assembled.
The latent heat term is applied as
\[
T^{\,n+1} \;=\; T^{\,n} + \Delta t\,\nabla^2_h T^{\,n}
                 \;+\; \kappa\big(\phi^{\,n+1}-\phi^{\,n}\big),
\tag{15.3}\]
that is, using the already updated \(\phi\) rather than a separate time derivative. This is a sequential rather than simultaneous update of the two fields, and it is deliberate: it matches the reference Julia implementation this application was validated against, so the two can be compared step-for-step.

title: 15  Kobayashi dendritic solidification
text:
15.4 Solution strategy
Explicit stepping. Halo exchange for two field groups per step — state and auxiliary — unless extended halos are requested, in which case a single wider exchange covers both. The GPU drivers keep working arrays resident on device and stage \(\phi\) and \(T\) to the host only for PNG output and verification.

title: 15  Kobayashi dendritic solidification
text:
15.5 Verification

Reference agreement. Checksums pinned against the reference implementation.
CPU–GPU parity. The CUDA 32²/4-step pin matches the CPU OpenMP pin; sum_T differs by 1 ULP.
Multi-rank. A two-rank variant is registered when MPI suites are on.

title: 15  Kobayashi dendritic solidification
text:
15.6 Binaries and inputs
kobayashi_fd_manual (MPI halos), kobayashi_fd_openmp (torus wrap plus OpenMP), plus CUDA and HIP drivers. Command-line driven, with PNG snapshots of \(\phi\).

15.7 Scalability
Not measured on LUMI-G. A 1-versus-2-GPU CUDA workflow exists for an H100 partition, but it is a two-point comparison rather than a strong-scaling curve and is not reported here as one.

title: 16  Scalability
text:
16.1 Method
All measurements are on LUMI-G, one MPI rank per GCD, double precision, I/O disabled, from the standard-g and dev-g partitions. The reported quantity is the median wall_step over accepted steps after a warm-up frame — the first frames include FFT planning and first-touch allocation and are not representative.
For a baseline of \(p_0 = 1\) GCD,
\[
S(p) \;=\; \frac{t(1)}{t(p)},
\qquad
E(p) \;=\; \frac{S(p)}{p}.
\tag{16.1}\]
Strong scaling means the global problem size is fixed while \(p\) grows, so the work per rank shrinks and the communication-to-computation ratio rises. Every curve here must therefore fall away from ideal eventually; the useful question is where, and why.
Raw data is committed under data/ and the figures are regenerated from it by figures/make_figures.py.

title: 16  Scalability
text:
16.4 Reading the comparison
The finite-difference curve is the best of the three at every rank count — 78% efficiency at one node against 59% for the spectral driver, and 47% against 38% at 32 GCDs. The reason is structural rather than incidental.
A finite-difference step communicates only with nearest neighbours: each rank exchanges a face with each neighbour, and the volume of that exchange falls as the subdomain shrinks. A distributed FFT communicates all-to-all: the transpose between decomposition axes moves data between every pair of ranks. As \(p\) grows, nearest-neighbour traffic stays local while all-to-all traffic grows, and the transpose comes to dominate the step.






What this comparison does and does not say



The two Heat3D drivers solve the same equation on the same machine, so comparing their scaling behaviour is legitimate, and the conclusion is that halo exchange strong-scales better than a distributed transpose.
It does not follow that finite differences are the better choice. The two runs are at different grid sizes (\(512^3\) against \(768^3\)) and, more importantly, the methods do not offer the same thing per step. The FD driver is explicit and bound by Equation 2.4; the spectral driver is unconditionally stable and can take a far larger timestep. Time-to-solution is the product of cost per step and number of steps, and this chapter measures only the first factor.
Nor does it license comparing either Heat3D driver against tungsten_hip: that is a different PDE with a different operator and a different amount of work per step.

title: 16  Scalability
section: 16.5 Where the curves stop being useful
text:
16.5 Where the curves stop being useful
All three fall below 50% efficiency by 24–32 GCDs. At \(768^3\) on 32 GCDs each rank holds roughly \(14\) million cells, and for the spectral models the transpose has become a substantial share of the step.
The practical readings are:

Up to one node (8 GCDs) every model is worth the resources.
Two to four nodes remain worthwhile for the largest grids, especially for the FD path.
Beyond that, at these grid sizes, further ranks buy progressively less. Extending the curve is better spent on a larger grid — weak scaling — than on more ranks at fixed size.

title: 17  Conclusions
text:
17.1 What the application set demonstrates
Thirteen applications, spanning fourth- through tenth-order spatial operators in the shipped spectral set, conserved and non-conserved dynamics, dispersive and dissipative behaviour, single- and multi-field systems, and both spectral and finite-difference discretisations — on one runtime, with one halo/decomposition layer and matching CPU and GPU paths.
The two claims from the abstract hold up, with qualifications worth stating.
High order is cheap to express. Chapter 7 (\(k^4\)), Chapter 6 (\(k^4\)), Chapter 8 (\(k^5\), imaginary), Chapter 9 (\(k^6\)) and Chapter 10 (\(k^{10}\)) differ, in their physics headers, by the polynomial one function returns. That is a real architectural result and not a presentational trick: none of these applications contains a loop over wave numbers, an MPI call, or a hand-written GPU kernel.
The qualification is that high order is not cheap to integrate. The stiffness grows as \(\Delta x^{-n}\), and the reason these models run at useful timesteps is Equation 2.3, not the spectral transform by itself. An explicit integrator on the sixth-order operator of Chapter 9 would need a timestep smaller by orders of magnitude.
The same source scales. Chapter 16 reports three measured curves out to 32 GCDs across four nodes, with checksums agreeing between 1 and 16 GCDs to between \(10^{-12}\) and \(3\times10^{-16}\). The application sources are unchanged between the one-GCD and 32-GCD runs.
The qualification is that all three curves fall below 50% efficiency by 24–32 GCDs at these grid sizes, and the report contains no weak-scaling study, which is the measurement that would actually justify a larger simulation.

title: 17  Conclusions
text:
17.2 The method comparison
The most useful single result is the pair of Heat3D curves, because they solve the same PDE. Halo exchange strong-scales better than a distributed transpose — 78% against 59% at one node — for the structural reason that nearest-neighbour communication stays local as ranks are added while an all-to-all transpose does not.
This does not make finite differences the better method. The spectral driver is unconditionally stable and takes a much larger timestep; the comparison here measures cost per step, not time to solution. Establishing the latter would require running both to a fixed accuracy, which has not been done.

title: 17  Conclusions
text:
17.3 Gaps
Honest accounting of what this report cannot support:

Ten of thirteen applications have no scaling measurement. The spectral ones share a stack with Chapter 3 and would be expected to track it, but expectation is not measurement.
No CPU control. Without a LUMI-C run at equal node count, the report cannot quantify what the GPU path buys.
No weak scaling. Every curve holds the problem fixed.
No time-to-solution comparison between the spectral and FD paths at matched accuracy — the comparison a user actually needs when choosing.
The two PFC applications have no analytical verification, only regression and self-consistency. This is inherent to a realistic equation of state, but it means their correctness rests on pinned checksums rather than closed-form agreement.

title: 17  Conclusions
text:
17.4 Suggested next measurements
In order of what would most improve this report:

A weak-scaling study on tungsten_hip — fixed cells per GCD, growing grid. This is the curve that says whether a larger science run is feasible, and it is the one currently missing.
Time-to-solution at matched accuracy for the two Heat3D drivers, which would turn Chapter 16’s method comparison into actionable guidance.
A LUMI-C CPU control at equal node count for one model.
One scaling point for a second spectral application — enough to test whether the shared-stack expectation actually holds.
